results.result: The cyk-4(or749ts) E448K mutation impairs membrane localization of CYK-4 in a temperature-sensitive manner. CYK-4ΔC1 (lacking the C1 domain) also fails to accumulate on ingressing cleavage furrows and gonad membranes, demonstrating that the C1 domain is required for membrane localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C64 are supported by imaging data in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 4 showing that both CYK-4E448K at restrictive temperature and CYK-4ΔC1 fail to localize to membranes. The temperature-sensitive nature of E448K membrane localization is directly demonstrated, and the C1 domain requirement is confirmed by deletion analysis.

results.result: CYK-4ΔC1 and CYK-4E448K embryos exhibit cytokinesis defects with slow and incomplete furrow ingression. In the absence of NOP-1, neither CYK-4ΔC1 nor CYK-4E448K support detectable furrow ingression, while CYK-4WT supports full ingression.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C69 are supported by kymograph data in Figure 1C-G showing quantitative furrow ingression kinetics. The data demonstrate that membrane localization via the C1 domain is essential for centralspindlin-dependent cytokinesis, particularly in the sensitized nop-1 background.

results.result: Loss of CED-10/Rac1 partially suppresses cytokinesis defects in cyk-4(or749ts) embryos but does not suppress defects in cyk-4ΔC1 embryos or in cyk-4E448K embryos when NOP-1 is compromised, suggesting CYK-4 does not act directly on CED-10.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C73 are supported by genetic interaction data in Figure 1E,H,I,J. The differential suppression patterns indicate that CED-10 inactivation provides only partial rescue and requires the NOP-1 pathway, arguing against CED-10 being the primary target of CYK-4 GAP activity.

results.result: The CYK-4R459A mutant (catalytic arginine substitution) retains the ability to bind RhoA•GTP but lacks detectable GAP activity towards both RhoA and CED-10/Rac1 in vitro.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77 are supported by biochemical data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and 2. The binding assays demonstrate proper protein folding, while GAP assays confirm loss of catalytic activity, validating this as a separation-of-function mutant.

results.result: cyk-4(ok1034) null embryos are lethal, but expression of GAP-deficient CYK-4R459A rescues embryonic lethality, producing viable but sterile adults. This demonstrates that CYK-4 GAP activity is not essential for post-embryonic development but is required for gonad development.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C80 are supported by phenotypic analysis in Figure 2A showing that CYK-4R459A provides significant rescue of embryonic lethality but not fertility. This establishes tissue-specific requirements for GAP activity.

results.result: Embryos expressing only CYK-4R459A proceed normally through early cell cycle stages and furrow ingression initiates at near wild-type rates, but cytokinesis fails to complete and furrows regress, suggesting a late step in cytokinesis is most sensitive to loss of CYK-4 GAP activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C84 are supported by time-lapse imaging and kymograph analysis in Figure 2B,C. The data show that CYK-4R459A localizes properly to the spindle midzone and supports near-complete furrow ingression before failure, indicating the GAP activity is specifically required for late cytokinesis.

results.result: CYK-4EE (K495E/R499E), which exhibits reduced RhoA binding in vitro, shows a stronger furrow ingression defect than CYK-4R459A. NOP-1 depletion from cyk-4EE embryos largely eliminates furrow ingression, demonstrating that Rho GTPase binding by CYK-4 is essential for centralspindlin-mediated cytokinesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C91 are supported by binding assays (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and kymograph analysis (Figure 3C,D). The more severe phenotype of CYK-4EE compared to CYK-4R459A indicates that GTPase binding is more critical than catalytic activity alone.

results.result: Mutation of CED-10/Rac1 or depletion of CDC-42 does not affect furrow ingression rates, even in nop-1 mutants. Cytokinesis proceeds to completion when NOP-1, CED-10/Rac1, and CDC-42 are simultaneously inactivated, indicating RhoA is the relevant GTPase that CYK-4 binds to promote furrow formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C95 are supported by kymograph data in Figure 3E,F. The ability of embryos to complete cytokinesis without CED-10, CDC-42, or NOP-1 demonstrates that these GTPases are not essential targets of CYK-4, implicating RhoA by elimination.

results.result: nop-1; cyk-4R459A double mutant embryos exhibit extremely weak furrow ingression (<10% of egg width), supporting models in which CYK-4 GAP activity is involved in RhoA activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C97 are supported by kymograph data in Figure 4B,C. The severe synthetic phenotype when both pathways are compromised provides strong genetic evidence that CYK-4 GAP activity promotes rather than inhibits RhoA activation.

results.result: Loss of CED-10/Rac1 partially rescues cyk-4R459A embryos (75% complete cytokinesis), but nop-1; ced-10; cyk-4R459A triple mutants completely fail to form ingressing furrows. Since the GAP active site is required even in the absence of CED-10/Rac1, CED-10/Rac1 inactivation cannot be the primary function of the CYK-4 GAP domain.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C104 are supported by genetic interaction data in Figure 4B,C and Figure 4—figure supplements 1-2. The triple mutant phenotype definitively demonstrates that CYK-4 GAP activity has an essential function distinct from CED-10/Rac1 inactivation.

results.result: Depletion of RGA-3/4 (a conventional RhoA GAP) causes hypercontractility in wild-type embryos but completely rescues cytokinesis in cyk-4R459A embryos and in nop-1; cyk-4R459A embryos (100% completion). This suppression is CYK-4-dependent and specific to cyk-4R459A, with CYK-4 mutants forming an allelic series: cyk-4R459A > cyk-4EE > cyk-4ΔC1 ≈ cyk-4(RNAi).
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C110 are supported by imaging and quantification in Figure 5B,C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1. The complete rescue by RGA-3/4 depletion provides strong evidence that CYK-4 GAP activity promotes RhoA activation, as removing the opposing GAP compensates for loss of CYK-4 function.

results.result: NMY-2::mRFP (myosin) accumulation is highly correlated with RhoA biosensor accumulation, providing a reliable proxy for RhoA activation. Mutations in CYK-4 that reduce furrow ingression also reduce myosin accumulation, with defects more severe in NOP-1-depleted embryos. RGA-3/4 depletion increases myosin accumulation in CYK-4R459A and CYK-4EE embryos.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C115 are supported by correlation analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) and quantification of myosin accumulation (Figure 5D,E). The correlation validates myosin as a RhoA activity readout, and the accumulation patterns support the model that CYK-4 GAP activity promotes RhoA activation.

results.result: A genetic suppressor screen of cyk-4(or749ts) isolated three suppressors from ~10^5 mutagenized genomes: one intragenic (H485Y in CYK-4) and two extragenic mutations in ect-2 (xs110: G707D in PH domain; xs111: E129K in BRCT linker). The ect-2(xs110) suppressor was confirmed as causative by CRISPR/Cas9 recreation and suppresses the primary defect of cyk-4(or749ts), restoring normal furrow initiation timing and ingression rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C123 are supported by genetic screen results, sequencing data (Figure 6A), phenotypic analysis (Figure 6B,C), and CRISPR validation. The rarity of suppressors and their specificity to ECT-2 activation strongly support the model that CYK-4's essential function is to activate RhoA via ECT-2.

results.result: ect-2(xs110) embryos exhibit hypercontractility during pseudocleavage and cytokinesis, associated with enhanced myosin accumulation. This is a dominant gain-of-function allele. The hypercontractility is reduced in ect-2(xs110); cyk-4(or749ts) embryos, indicating mutual suppression. ect-2(xs110) embryos also show defects in cleavage plane positioning but remain viable and fertile.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C130 are supported by imaging data in Figure 6B,D-F and Figure 6—figure supplements 3-4. The hypercontractility phenotype and its partial dependence on CYK-4 support the model that the G707D mutation hyperactivates ECT-2.

results.result: The second suppressor, ect-2(xs111) (E129K), exhibits similar characteristics to ect-2(xs110) but may be more strongly activated, as ect-2(xs111); cyk-4(or749ts); nop-1(RNAi) embryos fully ingress during cytokinesis (unlike comparable xs110 embryos). Completion depends on residual CYK-4E448K activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C135 are supported by phenotypic analysis in Figure 6B,C. The stronger suppression by xs111 compared to xs110 in the triple mutant background suggests differential activation levels, though both mutations activate ECT-2.

results.result: The genetic screen demonstrates that the essential function of CYK-4 inactivated by E448K is the ability to activate RhoA. CRISPR-generated cyk-4R459A strains combined with ect-2(xs110) or ect-2(xs111) exhibit high viability and fertility, confirming that the sole essential function of the RhoGAP active site is to stimulate ECT-2-mediated RhoA activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C139 are supported by the genetic screen results, viability data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), and CRISPR experiments (Figure 6B). The ability of hyperactive ECT-2 to bypass the requirement for CYK-4 GAP activity provides definitive genetic evidence for the proposed mechanism.

results.result: The catalytic C-terminal domains of CYK-4 and ECT-2 directly interact in vitro, and a similar complex is found with human orthologs.
results.evaluation: Claims C140-C141 are supported by GST pulldown assays in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1. The direct interaction between the catalytic domains provides biochemical support for the model that CYK-4 GAP activity directly modulates ECT-2 GEF activity.

results.result: Wild-type ECT-2 N- and C-termini form a complex in vitro. The E129K substitution (but not G707D) significantly reduces this binding, suggesting the ect-2(xs111) allele functions by relieving autoinhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C144 are supported by binding assays in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1. The differential effects of the two mutations on intramolecular binding provide mechanistic insight into how they activate ECT-2.

results.result: The ECT-2G707D variant exhibits a modest increase in GEF activity compared to wild-type ECT-2 over a range of concentrations, perhaps by increasing the affinity of ECT-2 for RhoA.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C146 are supported by GEF activity assays in Figure 7D. The modest increase in catalytic activity provides biochemical evidence for activation, though the mechanism (increased affinity) remains speculative.

results.result: CYK-4 has multiple functional domains required for RhoA activation: the C1 domain (membrane localization), RhoA binding capability, and catalytic GAP activity. For the GAP domain to promote RhoA activation, it must act catalytically on RhoA•GTP, implying RhoA plays a role in promoting its own activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C150 are supported by the comprehensive mutational analysis throughout the paper (Figures 1-5). The requirement for all three functions (membrane binding, GTPase binding, and catalytic activity) is demonstrated by the phenotypic severity hierarchy of the mutants.

results.result: The authors propose a working model in which the most active form of the ECT-2 RhoGEF is a complex containing ECT-2, CYK-4, and RhoA•GDP bound to the GAP active site. This implies CYK-4 GAP binds RhoA•GTP to form the active complex, suggesting a positive feedback loop where RhoA•GTP promotes RhoGEF activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C151, C153, C154 represent a proposed mechanistic model shown in Figure 7E. While the model is consistent with the genetic and biochemical data, direct biochemical evidence for the proposed ECT-2/CYK-4/RhoA•GDP complex is lacking. The authors acknowledge they could not detect GEF stimulation in vitro, possibly due to missing components or context. The model remains speculative pending structural or reconstitution studies.

results.result: Full activation of RhoA requires that the CYK-4 GAP domain both bind a Rho family GTPase and activate GTP hydrolysis. Mutations diminishing GTPase binding (CYK-4EE) exhibit stronger defects than mutation of the GAP active site (CYK-4R459A).
results.evaluation: Claims C155-C156 are supported by the allelic series data in Figure 5C showing cyk-4EE has more severe defects than cyk-4R459A. This demonstrates that both binding and catalysis are required, with binding being more critical.

results.result: CED-10/Rac1 is not the primary target for CYK-4 GAP activity. While loss of CED-10/Rac1 can partially restore cytokinesis completion in GAP-deficient embryos, the GAP active site is still required in the absence of CED-10/Rac1. The rescue by ced-10 mutation likely occurs through reduction of cortical tension, allowing increased NOP-1-dependent furrow ingression.
results.evaluation: Claims C163-C167 are supported by the genetic interaction data in Figure 4B showing that nop-1; ced-10; cyk-4R459A triple mutants fail completely. The proposed mechanism involving cortical tension is supported by citation to prior work (Loria et al., 2012) and is consistent with the data.

results.result: CYK-4 GAP activity promotes RhoA activation and is essential in early C. elegans embryos and adult germline. Post-embryonically, the requirement is relaxed, as GAP-deficient CYK-4R459A supports development to viable but sterile adults. The requirement can be experimentally eliminated by ECT-2 hyperactivation or RGA-3/4 depletion. RGA-3/4 is primarily expressed in germline and early embryos, potentially explaining tissue-specific requirements.
results.evaluation: Claims C168-C171 are supported by the rescue experiments (Figure 2A), suppression data (Figures 5B, 6B), and expression data (cited from NextDB). The tissue-specific requirements are well-documented, though the mechanistic explanation involving RGA-3/4 expression remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: The findings reconcile previous conflicting results about CYK-4 GAP function. Some cell types may not require GAP activity (as in post-embryonic C. elegans cells). Results suggesting CYK-4 GAP attenuates Rac1 may be indirect effects of reduced RhoA activation or altered cortical tension, since active RhoA can indirectly inhibit Rac1. Many previous results can be explained without proposing different functions in different organisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C172-C174 provide a synthesis of the current findings with prior literature. The interpretation is well-supported by the data and citations (particularly Guilluy et al., 2011 review on RhoA-Rac1 crosstalk). The context-dependent requirements demonstrated in this study provide a framework for understanding previous discrepancies.

results.result: The signaling mechanisms discovered have analogies in other pathways. The proposed RhoA positive feedback is reminiscent of Cdc42 activation during yeast budding and SOS1 RasGEF activation by Ras•GTP. Similarly, p115 RhoGEF is activated by Gα13, with its RGS domain (a Gα GAP) stabilizing Gα13 binding to the GEF domain. Additional cases of GAP domains promoting GEF activity may have gone undetected.
results.evaluation: Claims C176-C184 draw well-supported analogies to other signaling systems with appropriate citations (Howell and Lew, 2012; Gureasko et al., 2008; Chen et al., 2012; Tesmer et al., 1997). The comparison to p115 RhoGEF is particularly apt and illustrated in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B. The speculation about undetected cases is reasonable given the counterintuitive nature of the mechanism.

results.result: RhoA activation during cytokinesis is controlled by multiple layers of regulation including cell-cycle regulated phosphorylation of CYK-4 and ECT-2, membrane binding by CYK-4 (requiring centralspindlin oligomerization), and GAP/GEF activities. The requirement for the C1 domain is context-dependent: major in C. elegans embryos but not essential in HeLa cells. Not all cell types may require maximal ECT-2 activation due to differences in physical or biochemical properties, but evolutionary conservation suggests critical roles during metazoan development.
results.evaluation: Claims C185-C193 provide a comprehensive summary of the regulatory complexity, supported by data throughout the paper and appropriate citations. The context-dependent requirements are well-documented, and the evolutionary argument is sound. The speculation about why requirements vary (C192) is reasonable but remains to be tested.
